clue.text: Picture covering Queen's long continuing story

indicators.note: A cover lies over a thing on both sides, so the short piece ends up wrapped inside the word in front of it.

parts.note: to picture something is to see it in your mind
Qu. is the standard short form for a queen, as in Qu. Victoria
l is the abbreviation for long, the letter on a clothing label

explanation.surface: A film telling the long-running story of the Queen's reign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picture' is a noun everywhere in the surface — a film about royalty — and a verb in the wordplay, the everyday sense of seeing a thing in your head.
explanation.definitionFit: continuing story → SEQUEL: the book or film that carries an earlier story onward, a story continued rather than a fresh one.

clue.text: Select spreadsheet program and occasionally alter books

parts.note: Microsoft's spreadsheet is the one everybody names

indicators.note: Something done occasionally happens at intervals rather than every time, so only every other letter of the word beside it is picked up.

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of aLtEr
NT is the New Testament, the crossword's usual books

explanation.surface: Choosing a spreadsheet package and now and then quietly fiddling with the accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Books' is the New Testament in most clues that use it, while the surface has it as the ledgers somebody is altering.
explanation.definitionFit: Select → EXCELLENT: 'select' in the sense of choice, picked out as the best, as in a select few rather than the verb.

clue.text: At university, go for advancement

parts.note: a British student in residence at Oxford or Cambridge is said to be up
your go in a game is your turn

explanation.surface: Advice to a student: aim high while you are still at university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go for' reads as one phrase, the encouragement to chase something, and its two words belong to different halves of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: advancement → UPTURN: a turn upwards in fortunes, the noun for things improving after a flat stretch.

clue.text: Bury put ultimate market on street behind Rock

indicators.note: The ultimate thing in a series is the final one, so only the closing letter of the word beside it is wanted.
Whatever stands behind a thing comes after it, so those two letters follow the piece just named.

parts.note: to put something down is to lay it

indicators.note: In a down clue whatever is placed on something else is written above it, so this piece goes in first.

parts.note: the last letter of markeT
ore is rock with metal in it, hacked out of a mine
st is the standard abbreviation on any address

explanation.surface: Bury's last market being moved to the street behind the rock venue.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town in Greater Manchester, which is what the capital letter and the market are for, and the definition is the plain verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Bury → LAY TO REST: the gentle phrase used of a funeral, where saying 'bury' outright would sound blunt.

clue.text: Fine scientific establishment busy cutting American slack

parts.note: f is the grade stamped on a fine pencil
a lab is where the science actually gets done
American is US, and BUSY with those two cut out of it leaves B…Y

explanation.surface: A first-rate laboratory hard at work trimming the slack out of an American budget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' opens as praise for the laboratory and is a single letter, the grade printed on the side of a pencil.
explanation.definitionFit: slack → FLABBY: loose and lacking firmness, the sense of slack used of a rope or a waistline rather than an idle worker.

clue.text: Fare well, finally plugging major leak

indicators.note: What comes finally is at the end, so the closing letter of the word before it is the one taken.

parts.note: fare is what is set before you at table

indicators.note: A plug is pushed into a hole, so this letter goes inside the word rather than alongside it.

parts.note: the last letter of welL

explanation.surface: Saying goodbye while at last getting round to stopping a burst pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare well' looks like a farewell split in two, and 'fare' is the old word for the food put in front of a guest.
explanation.definitionFit: major leak → FLOOD: water escaping in overwhelming quantity, a leak scaled up until it fills the room.

clue.text: Repel extra-terrestrial assault that's drained earth

parts.note: the ordinary word for a being from another planet

indicators.note: A thing drained has had its middle emptied out, leaving only what sat at either end of the word.

parts.note: the outside letters of AssaulT, its middle poured away
E marks the earth wire in a plug

explanation.surface: Fighting off an attack from space that has left the planet dried out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extra-terrestrial assault' reads as one phrase off a science-fiction poster, and the two words are separate pieces of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Repel → ALIENATE: to drive people away by making them hostile, repelling in the social sense rather than the physical one.

clue.text: Starters in Bengal have additional jhalmuri in side dish

indicators.note: A starter comes first, so the opening letter of each word that follows is what the clue hands over.

parts.note: the opening letters of those five words, taken in the order given

explanation.surface: An Indian meal where puffed-rice snacks arrive with something extra alongside.
explanation.walkthrough: Jhalmuri is a Bengali street snack of spiced puffed rice, so the sentence reads as a genuine menu — which is what hides the run of initials.
explanation.definitionFit: side dish → BHAJI: the deep-fried onion fritter served beside an Indian main course, a dish that only ever turns up on the side.

clue.text: Silently cheers Leicester perhaps securing lead in League

indicators.note: To secure something is to hold it fast inside, so the letter goes within the word rather than after it.

parts.note: ta is the British thank-you, and cheers does the same job when a drink is handed over

indicators.note: The lead is whatever goes in front, so the first letter of the word following is the one taken.

parts.note: Leicester City is the football club, so 'perhaps' offers the town as one example of the word that follows it
the first letter of League

explanation.surface: Fans quietly cheering Leicester as the club takes top place in the league.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole sentence is football, and 'cheers' is not the noise from the terraces but the word you say when somebody buys you a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Silently → TACITLY: done without saying it aloud, the way a tacit agreement is one nobody ever spoke.

clue.text: Cutlery with carved apostles on captivating bishop

definitions.note: Cutlery is a mass noun covering knives, forks and spoons together, so it names a set of items where the answer names several of one kind.

indicators.note: Carving cuts a thing into fresh shapes, so the letters beside it are cut into a different order.
To captivate is to hold somebody captive, so the shuffled letters close around the single letter named.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters
B is the bishop on a chess board

explanation.surface: Church silverware showing the carved apostles, with a bishop worked into the design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carved apostles' sounds like church woodwork and 'on' passes for a preposition, so the word that looks least like fodder is part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutlery → TABLESPOONS: the knives, forks and spoons of a place setting, tablespoons being the large ones, so an example of cutlery.

clue.text: Paper craft has old sails etc, one master recalled

parts.note: a ship's rig is its sails, masts and rigging, hence the etc

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the letters of one and master come back in reverse order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
MA is a Master of Arts degree

explanation.surface: A nautical paper hobby: someone folds a model of an old sailing ship and remembers a former skipper.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'recalled' about memory of a ship's captain, but it means called back: 'one master' is reversed to give AMI at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding sheets into shapes such as cranes and boats, a craft done with paper.

clue.text: Stuff for recipe needs vigorous tenderising

definitions.note: Stuff is a mass noun naming the material as a whole, so it does not agree in number with the plural answer it stands for.

indicators.note: A vigorous action is a violent shaking-about, and letters shaken that hard do not come back in the order they went in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters — the same count as the enumeration

explanation.surface: A cook beating a tough cut of meat hard before it goes into the pot.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word here belongs to the kitchen, so the one doing letter work reads as ordinary cookery, and it is the longest word in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuff for recipe → INGREDIENTS: the things a recipe lists, 'stuff' being the informal word for the material something is made from.

clue.text: Strictly's content to condemn canoodling and mostly blame Romeo

indicators.note: to condemn something is to damn or wreck it, so the letters are torn up and rebuilt
most of the word blame, so its last letter goes

parts.note: R is Romeo in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A tabloid fuss about kissing and blame among the contestants on a TV dance show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims BLAME to BLAM; with CANOODLING and R these letters are rearranged. Strictly Come Dancing is the BBC's celebrity dance contest.
explanation.definitionFit: The waltzes, tangos and foxtrots on Strictly Come Dancing are all forms of ballroom dancing, the show's subject matter.

clue.text: Pitcher Webb, initially retained by phone company, gets sponsor in the end

indicators.note: Initially means at the very start, so only the opening letter of the name is used.
To retain something is to keep hold of it inside, so the letter sits within the word that follows.

parts.note: EE is one of Britain's big mobile networks

indicators.note: The end is where a word's last letter lives, so that closing letter is the one taken.

parts.note: the first letter of the surname
the last letter of sponsoR

explanation.surface: A baseball pitcher called Webb kept on by a phone firm until a sponsor steps in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitcher' is a baseball player in the surface and a jug in the definition, and the phone company is EE, a British network a solver elsewhere would never have met.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitcher → EWER: the tall wide-lipped jug that stands on a washstand, pitcher in its water-carrying sense.

clue.text: Engineers dubiously accept abridged permit for vessel

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps

indicators.note: done in a doubtful, irregular way, so the letters of accept are shuffled
cut short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: to let is to permit

explanation.surface: Army engineers grudgingly take a shortened permit for a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessel' looks like a ship in this naval-sounding surface, but here it means a container such as a jug or bowl. RE for the Royal Engineers is a standard crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A receptacle is a container, and vessel can mean any container such as a jug or bowl.

clue.text: Trusting a silly order to enter rising river

definitions.note: Trusting is the adjective of 'a trusting soul', which is how it stands in for a phrase describing a person rather than for a verb.

indicators.note: To order things is to put them in an arrangement, so those letters come out in an arrangement of the setter's choosing.

parts.note: the Dee runs through Aberdeen and past Chester, and it is climbing here

indicators.note: Entering something means going inside it, so this group is placed within the other rather than after it.
A down entry read upwards climbs the grid, so the word said to be rising arrives back to front.

parts.note: those six letters rearranged and dropped inside

explanation.surface: Somebody obeying a foolish command to sail up a swollen river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trusting a silly order' reads as one continuous phrase, a soldier doing as he is told, and the definition stops after its first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Trusting → EASILY LED: someone easily led believes whatever they are told, which is trusting taken as far as gullible.

clue.text: Company mounts scheme engaging a space traveller

indicators.note: the reordered letters take in the a, holding it inside
to scheme is to plot or rearrange, so the letters of mounts are reordered

explanation.surface: A firm sets up a plan involving a rocket launch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mounts' reads as a verb in the surface, but it is just letters to be reordered, and 'scheme' is a verb telling you to plot them anew.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosmonaut is a Russian or Soviet astronaut, someone who travels into space.

clue.text: Conflict with detective on plan for future

indicators.note: In a down clue whatever sits on something else is written above it, so these two letters go in first.

parts.note: DI is a detective inspector, the rank in every British police drama
a leader's vision is the future they intend to bring about

explanation.surface: A row with the detective about what the plan should be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conflict with detective' reads as a quarrel involving the police, which is where the definition ends: only its first word belongs to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Conflict → DIVISION: a split between people who disagree, conflict in the sense of a party divided rather than a battle.

clue.text: Some fellowship at riot is misrepresented as love for one's country

indicators.note: Only some of what follows is wanted — a run of letters inside those words rather than what they mean.

parts.note: the letters run consecutively from inside the first word across to the start of the last, in the order given

explanation.surface: A group's friendship at a riot being spun into something it never was.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue accuses somebody of misrepresenting a fellowship, which reads as political commentary, and its first word is the only one telling you to look at letters.
explanation.definitionFit: love for one’s country → PATRIOTISM: the noun for exactly that devotion, the word a dictionary offers for loving one's nation.

clue.text: It's a revolution in sparkling wine

indicators.note: A revolution turns a thing full circle, so what comes before it is read the other way round.

parts.note: the opening two words run together as four letters before anything is done to them

explanation.surface: A breakthrough being announced in the world of fizzy wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's a revolution' is the sort of line a wine advert uses, so the two words that carry the letters look like a verdict on something rather than material.
explanation.definitionFit: sparkling wine → ASTI: the sweet fizz from the Italian town of Asti, so the definition names the class it is one example of.

clue.text: Former president managed to hide confusion of age

indicators.note: the managing word hides the muddled letters inside it

parts.note: to run something is to manage it, so managed is ran

indicators.note: a confusion of the word age means its letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A former leader succeeded in covering up his muddled old age.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nods to talk of Reagan's age while in office; 'managed' gives the past tense ran, as in ran a company.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronald Reagan was the 40th President of the United States, serving from 1981 to 1989.

clue.text: On rare occasions previously writer worked, unable to be idle

parts.note: previously means at some earlier time

indicators.note: Dough that is worked is pushed about until it takes a new shape, and the letters beside it are handled the same way.

parts.note: the setter writing the clue refers to himself as I
the other six letters of the fodder, taken as they stand
somebody idling about is said to be mooning around

explanation.surface: A writer who used to put in some work and now cannot sit still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' as I is a standing crossword trick, the setter slipping himself into his own clue, and here he arrives as the person who worked.
explanation.definitionFit: On rare occasions → ONCE IN A BLUE MOON: the idiom for something that hardly ever happens, a blue moon being a rare second full moon in a month.

clue.text: Rage about variable care organised

indicators.note: the reordered letters go round the variable
the letters of care are put into a new order

parts.note: Z is a standard letter for a variable in algebra

explanation.surface: Fury over how variable care has been arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organised' turns CARE into CRAE, which goes 'about' Z. 'Rage' here is a fashion, as in all the rage.
explanation.definitionFit: A rage is a passing fashion everyone is mad about, exactly what a craze is.

clue.text: Put up partial screen or partition that protects clothing

indicators.note: In a down clue putting something up runs it back towards the top of the grid, so those letters read the other way.
Only part of what follows is wanted: a run of letters inside the words, not the words themselves.

parts.note: five letters in a row straddle the join between the first two words, and they are climbing

explanation.surface: Putting up a bit of screening to divide one room into two.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screen or partition' reads as the setter offering two words for the same object, which is the disguise: neither of them is defining anything.
explanation.definitionFit: that protects clothing → APRON: the garment tied over your clothes to keep the cooking off them, defined here by the job it does.

clue.text: Increasingly tentative, I ask her out

indicators.note: Something out of place is not where it was put, so those letters are set down somewhere other than where they started.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Somebody losing their nerve while working up to asking a woman out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ask her out' is one phrase in the surface, a man plucking up courage, and its last word is the instruction the letters need.
explanation.definitionFit: Increasingly tentative → SHAKIER: less steady than before, the comparative covering unsteady hands and an argument losing its footing alike.

clue.text: Preserve records admitting gridlocks

indicators.note: To admit somebody is to let them in, so the word in front opens up and takes the other one inside.

parts.note: a ship's log is the record kept of a voyage
jam is fruit preserved in sugar

explanation.surface: Keeping the files that own up to how badly the traffic seized up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preserve' opens as the verb the sentence seems to need and is the thing in the jar, the noun a crossword reaches for whenever preserves are mentioned.
explanation.definitionFit: gridlocks → LOGJAMS: blockages nothing can move through, from timber jammed in a river, used of traffic and stalled talks alike.

clue.text: Check information held by inner assembly

indicators.note: Held by something means kept inside it, so this letter sits within the group rather than beside it.
To assemble is to put parts together in a new arrangement, so the letters of the word before it are built up afresh.

parts.note: the five letters of INNER built up in a new order
i is the letter on every tourist information sign

explanation.surface: Checking a fact that one of the inner circle brought to the meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inner assembly' reads as a select committee, the small group inside a bigger one, and neither word means anything of the sort here.
explanation.definitionFit: Check → REIN IN: to hold something back the way a rider pulls on the reins, check in the sense of curbing rather than examining.

clue.text: Typify reactionary public school education

indicators.note: A reactionary wants everything to go back the way it came, so these letters are entered in the opposite direction.

parts.note: Eton is the best known of the fee-paying boarding schools the British confusingly call public schools
ed is the standard abbreviation, as in the Department for Education

explanation.surface: A backward-looking view of how the private schools educate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Public school' means the opposite in Britain to what it means everywhere else — a fee-paying private school — and Eton is the one setters reach for.
explanation.definitionFit: Typify → DENOTE: to stand for something as its sign, the sense in which a symbol denotes the thing it represents.
